lesson_title: Measurement and Maps Practice Run at Examination Pace
hook_text: Feed the formula a diameter instead of a radius and your drum grows FOUR times too big.
clip_script: The measurement practice paper is the practical one — a road, a hall, a drum — and its marks sit on the crossings. Watch. The N2, Gqeberha to East London, 310 kilometres at 100: that's 3,1 hours. NOT 3 hours 10 minutes — the decimal times sixty is 6. The clock runs on sixties; that one conversion carries its own mark. Now the youth centre: four walls, 102 square metres — minus the doors and windows, 89,4 — times two coats, 178,8 — divided by 8 per litre, 22,35 litres. The shop sells 10-litre tins: 2,235 becomes THREE tins, rounded UP, because two tins leaves bare wall and no one sells a quarter of a tin. Then times R899: R2 697 — and the budget of R2 500 falls R197 short. Say both numbers. The drum trap: the formula wants the RADIUS. Hand it the 0,8 metre diameter and your answer doesn't double — it QUADRUPLES, because the error gets squared. Halve first: 0,4, and the honest drum holds about 452 litres. And the crate: count whole boxes along each side — 4 by 3 by 5 is 60 — because volume division is only a ceiling, and part of a box ships nothing. Units on every line, times sixty, round up at the shop door. That's the practical paper, walked at exam pace.
visual_style: A highway strip map unrolling with a giant comma splitting 3,1 into hours and minutes; youth centre walls unfolding flat like cardboard while areas subtract themselves; a drum inflating to absurd size then snapping back when the diameter halves; boxes clicking into a crate in a 4-by-3-by-5 grid.
pacing: Brisk highway opening, steady beat through the painting chain, dramatic pause on the quadrupling drum, crisp counted finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full practice run and take the practical paper's 150 marks one clean crossing at a time.
